speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF SALE OF 120,000,000 BUSHELS TO UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish
to announce that negotiations which have been going on for some time between the Canadian wheat board and the United Kingdom ministry of food have resulted in the sale of one hundred and twenty million bushels of wheat futures for delivery during the period ending May, 1942. This is the largest single wheat transaction in the histoiy of the world's grain trade.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. HANSON (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF SALE OF 120,000,000 BUSHELS TO UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
Would the minister enlighten the
house as to the price or prices that have been fixed, if any?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF SALE OF 120,000,000 BUSHELS TO UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
The United Kingdom ministry of food informed us that they would require the same assurances as those they had last year; that is, that the prices to be paid will not be disclosed, and that the market will remain open during the period of the transaction.

I thought the house might be interested in a telegram which has been received on behalf of the British government from the Secretary of State for Dominion Affairs:
London, May 2, 1941.
High Commissioner for Canada has informed us of further wide and substantial tariff concessions on United Kingdom goods for which the Canadian budget provides. We appreciate to the full the magnitude and generosity of these measures which are yet another example of Canada's wholehearted cooperation. We attach the greatest value to our export trade with Canada, and, within the limits of our resources, no effort will be spared to take every advantage 0f these concessions for which we wish to express our most grateful thanks.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: REPRESENTATIONS OF TWENTY-NINE MEN WHO SERVED IN 1914-18 AS TO REFUSAL OF EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of National Defence. My question is based upon a communication which I have just received from Quebec city and which is signed by twenty-nine war veterans who give their serial numbers and their years of service in the great war of 1914-18. These veterans claim that they have made numerous attempts in the last few months to obtain employment in the various war sendees, which requests have been turned down because they were not known as partisans of the Liberal party. I table this communication for the minister's information. My question is: Is the government aware of this state of things, and will it tolerate it any longer?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. RALSTON (Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
subtopic: REPRESENTATIONS OF TWENTY-NINE MEN WHO SERVED IN 1914-18 AS TO REFUSAL OF EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: My answer to my hon. friend is that the government is not aware of that state of affairs, and in my opinion it is absolutely incorrect.

subtopic: REPRESENTATIONS OF TWENTY-NINE MEN WHO SERVED IN 1914-18 AS TO REFUSAL OF EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: How can the Minister of National Defence say that the statement of these war veterans in Quebec is incorrect?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
subtopic: REPRESENTATIONS OF TWENTY-NINE MEN WHO SERVED IN 1914-18 AS TO REFUSAL OF EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: I do not think my hon. friend is entitled to ask another question on the same point. What I say to him is this: When it is stated that veterans are refused employment, if it is in government services, because of the political views they hold, in my opinion that statement is absolutely incorrect.

subtopic: REPRESENTATIONS OF TWENTY-NINE MEN WHO SERVED IN 1914-18 AS TO REFUSAL OF EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: That is what they say in their petition.

subtopic: UTILIZATION OF CANADA CAR COMPANY PLANT AT AMHERST, N.S.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask a question of the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) based upon a telegram which I received this morning from a union official with reference to the mills of the Canada Car Company at Amherst, as well as to the aeroplane plant there. As I have sent a copy of this wire to the minister, there is no necessity of reading it. This matter has been brought to the attention of the minister several times in the past, and I should like to ask if he has any definite plans to utilize these plants, so that men may be employed in them to the best advantage in serving the country.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Munitions and Supply):
speakerposition: Minister of Munitions and Supply
subtopic: UTILIZATION OF CANADA CAR COMPANY PLANT AT AMHERST, N.S.
speechtext: The steel mill at Amherst is quite an old mill with no primary steel capacity. No situation has developed as yet in connection with which this steel mill could be usefully employed in war work. The aeroplane plant has received a large order, and I assume that the owners are developing the plant as rapidly as possible. A number of men have been training in Montreal for Amherst, and the jig and die work has been completed and sent down there. I think that as far as aeroplane work goes, employment will increase steadily, but I have no anticipation of larger employment in the steel mills.

subtopic: UTILIZATION OF CANADA CAR COMPANY PLANT AT AMHERST, N.S.
speechtext: Is there any possibility of utilizing these men somewhere else?

speakerposition: Minister of Munitions and Supply
subtopic: UTILIZATION OF CANADA CAR COMPANY PLANT AT AMHERST, N.S.
speechtext: Certainly.

I should like to reply to the question asked yesterday by the hon. member for Waterloo South (Mr. Homuth) with regard to the natural gas situation in western Ontario. I shall table a report on this matter as soon as it can be obtained, but in the meantime I can say that the power controller and the oil controller have been in active negotiation recently in an effort to augment the supply of gas for the coming winter. I have been informed verbally that arrangements have been completed which will, I think, bring about a more satisfactory condition in the supply of natural gas in western Ontario.

It will be noted that the same minima prices are fixed for the provinces of British Columbia, Ontario, Quebec, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia. These provinces, with the exception of Prince Edward Island, are all importers of butter, and Prince Edward Island's surplus is only approximately 500,000 pounds annually. Prices two cents per pound lower are fixed for the provinces of Alberta and Manitoba, and prices three cents

per pound lower for the province of Saskatchewan than for the other six provinces. These three provinces are exporting provinces, and the differentials provided are based upon existing freight rates to the principal markets of the exporting provinces.
Provision is made in the order for a minimum differential between solids and prints of one cent per pound. The average differential in Ontario and Quebec, in which provinces

Excise Act
about two-thirds of our butter is consumed, is approximately one cent per pound. It will be noticed that the minima prices are on a basis "of delivered to the purchaser," and it is felt that this is the only way in which fair competition in selling can be secured. It is felt that increases in the fixed minima prices from time to time, that is of one-half cent per month, throughout the production season will induce trading and support of the market by those who ordinarily store butter.
In accordance with the authority conferred by order in council, P.C. 3230, of May 10, 1941, the dairy products board has issued order No. 21. With the consent of the house I should like to place this on Hansard. It is: Order No. 21
The dairy products board hereby orders that
1.	For the purposes of this order
(a)	"Solid" or "solids" shall mean creamery butter solidly packed in boxes containing a net weight of approximately fifty-six pounds or more.
(b)	"Prints" or "rolls" shall mean packages of creamery butter of net weight of one-quarter pound, one-half pound, one pound or multiples thereof.
(c)	A "dairy produce broker" is one who does not warehouse or handle dairy products but acts as an intermediary between buyer and seller, selling on a brokerage basis.
(d)	A "dairy product commission agent" is one who warehouses and sells dairy products for the owner on a commission basis.
(e)	"Delivered to the purchaser" shall mean f.o.b. destination as mutually agreed between vendor and purchaser.
2.	No person shall sell or purchase first grade creamery butter in any province in Canada at prices below those specified in schedule No. 1 annexed hereto, for the month and province in which the same occurs. Sales shall be on a basis of the butter sold being delivered to the purchaser at the expense of the vendor.
3.	No vendor shall allow and no purchaser shall accept any discount or other consideration on account of the sale or purchase of first grade creamery butter, which would have the effect of reducing the net returns to the vendors below those specified in schedule No. 1 provided,
(a)	that if a dairy produce broker or dairy produce commission agent is actually engaged in any transaction, brokerage or commission fees at recognized rates may be allowed, and
(b)	brokerage fees shall be paid direct to the broker by either the vendor or the purchaser as may be agreed.
4.	If butter inferior in quality to first grade is sold at prices below those specified in schedule No. 1 such butter shall be correctly marked as to grade in accordance with the provisions of the regulations under the Dairy Industry Act respecting grade standards and sizes of type required for designating grades.
The foregoing order will be in effect from the date of publication thereof in the Canada Gazette.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
These
resolutions respecting the Excise Act need not take very long, but I think the minister should give the committee some explanation in regard to them. Perhaps he will put on the record the previous rates, the receipts by years over a period of years, and the revenue anticipated in the coming year. I should like the same detail with respect to malt and spirits.
While I am on the subject of spirits I would ask the minister to make plain just what the taxes on spirits are in Canada-customs, excise and what-not-so that the public may understand just how much of the purchase price of a bottle of whisky goes to the government. There is a substantial opinion in the country -it has reached me from every section of Canada-that the government in raising money by taxation should have resorted to further taxes on spirits, and in justice to the government itself I think the position should be made quite clear. Has the taxation on spirits reached such a point that it is thought that the law of diminishing returns may 'be in effect? I have an open mind on this question, but I do know that there is a substantial body of public opinion

no doubt it has been expressed to the minister-which objects to the government's not having increased the tax on spirits. There may be a good reason for it, but the whole position should be clarified.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Answering the first part of the question relating to beer, the present rates and the proposed rates of duty for malt, beer, and malt syrup are as follows: On malt, domestic, the present rate is 10 cents per pound and the proposed rate 12 cents per pound. On malt, imported, the present rate is 10 cents per pound and the proposed rate 12 cents per pound. The yield from those taxes-

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: On malt alone?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
On malt alone, which is by far the main part of the beer taxes-nearly all of the taxes on beer are raised by the duty on malt. The malt duties to which I have referred yielded in the fiscal year 1940-41, 816,802,539.80. The estimated increase antici-

pated as a result of the new rate of 12 cents per pound is $3,360,507.96, so that the estimated yield from the malt duties for the present fiscal year 1941-42 is $20,163,047.76- which is a fine estimate, I may say.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The minister must expect an increased consumption.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes. The duties on beer are unimportant, but I had better give them to complete the story. The present rate on beer, dutiable, is 30 cents per gallon, and the proposed rate, 35 cents per gallon. The present rate on beer, imported, is 7 cents per gallon, and the proposed rate, 12 cents per gallon. The yield-

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Before the minister goes on, when he speaks of duty, is he speaking of excise?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Is there in addition a customs duty on beer?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: On imported beer, yes.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: On imported beer; and is that the item referred to in section 3 (b), or is it only excise?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
These are excise duties.
There is a duty in the customs tariff which is separate from these.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
What is
the customs tariff on beer and malt?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am sorry I have not that information, but it does not make very much difference because there is practically no beer imported. Beer is a domestic product.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Does any ale or porter come under this? They are under the definition of beer?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Surely
we import some Guinness' stout and porter, do we not?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Very little. It is infinitesimal compared with the consumption of beer. The yield from beer, dutiable, in the fiscal year 1940-41 was $411,970.98, and the increased rate of duty is estimated to yield an increase of $68,661.83, making a total yield from that source for the present fiscal year of $480,632.81.
On beer, imported, the present rate is 7 cents per gallon and the proposed rate, 12 cents per gallon. The yield in 1940-41 was $6,874.96, and the increase is estimated at $4,910.68, making an estimated total yield of $11,785.64.
On malt syrup the present domestic rate is 15 cents per pound, and the proposed rate is

Excise Act
18 cents per pound. The yield in 1940-41 was $98,951.53, and the estimated increase due to the higher rate is $19,531.56, making a total estimated yield of $118,483.09.
On malt syrup, imported, the present rate is 25 cents per pound, and the proposed rate is 30 cents per pound. The yield in 1940-41, partly at 21 cents and partly at 25 cents per pound, was $9,729.41; the estimated increase due to the higher rate is, for the present fiscal year, $2,211.05, making an estimated total yield of $11,940.46.
Of course, the estimates for the present year, while I have given them down to a cent, will not, being estimates, work out just that way; they are approximations.
The hon. gentleman asked me about spirits. The excise duty on spirits is $7 per gallon.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
What is
the customs duty?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The British preferential
rate is $8 per gallon, and the general rate is $10 per gallon.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Eight
dollars?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Eight dollars, coming from
Great Britain.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Fifteen
dollars per gallon, the two together?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No. That is not it. It is
only $7 per gallon on the domestic product and $8 a gallon when imported from Great Britain.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
There is
the sales tax in addition to that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Any other tax?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: There is either the excise in the case of domestic production, or the customs of $8 in the case of importations.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Plus the sales tax in either event?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is true.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: That is the dominion tax?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: How does that work out per imperial quart?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Perhaps I had better take a little time and get that accurately.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The idea of asking these questions is to ascertain and to give to the public the exact facts with relation to taxation on spirits and beer. I think it would be useful information to give to the public.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
There is, as I stated, a demand that the rate of taxation on liquor of one form or another be increased in war time. Now, is that based on a practical state of affairs? I am not speaking in any sense of prohibition, or liquor control, or anything of the sort; I am seeking to learn whether it is practicable that we in Canada should put further taxes on spirits. If the minister cannot answer that now, he will be good enough to do it later.
What will be the effect of the increased tax on malt, on beer, and on malt syrup, on the price (a) of a glass of beer, (b) of a bottle of beer, (c) of a case of beer? What increased contribution are the consumers of beer to make to the national treasury in time of war: I will put it that way. The brewing business is a legitimate business, but, I suggest, it is in the luxury class. Although in England beer is looked upon as a staple, in Canada it is not quite in the same class. I merely wish to ascertain the true position, without making any reflection on anybody or seeking to drive the government into any other position. Will there be an increase in the price of beer to the consuming public, and how much will it be, and should it not be more?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Let me take these two questions in their order. The first relates to spirits. As I said before, the duty on spirits is now $7.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: That is the excise?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The excise duty is $7 and the import duty is $8.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: We have that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The excise duty was raised from $4 in September of 1939 to $7-needless to say, a substantial increase.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Some of the provinces, including Ontario, shortly or immediately after we raised the duty on spirits from $4 to $7 in the fall of 1939, also raised their mark-up on spirits, which in effect amounted to an increase in the provincial tax to correspond or practically correspond with the increase in the dominion tax. The result of that was that the sales of spirits in the liquor stores of
Excise Act

Ontario dropped off to a marked degree. Not only that; I was informed that smuggling of spirits into Ontario began to take on proportions, and this was regarded as sufficiently serious to justify the Ontario liquor commission in lowering its mark-up of spirits, which they did in November or December of 1939. This incident was taken by us, and I am sure by the government of Ontario, as indicating that the taxes on spirits, whether by way of dominion excise duty or of provincial mark-up, could not safely be raised without danger of increased illicit importation, illicit manufacture in Canada through stills and so on, and of course, illicit sales.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Bootlegging.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes. These are the main considerations which led us at this time not to increase the duty on spirits.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Having
already raised them a year ago.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Having already raised them so largely in the fall of 1939. I believe I stated in my budget speech that the consumption of spirits had not increased. I find that it increased somewhat, but not to any marked degree. The total proof gallons of domestic and foreign matured spirits entered for consumption for the fiscal year 1939-40 was 3.645,892.74. The quantity for the fiscal year 1940-41 was 3,850,238.82, showing a very small proportionate increase in the consumption of spirits. That is contrary to the impression which a good many persons in the country have, and it is in contrast to the large increase in the consumption of beer.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: There has been a large increase in the consumption of beer?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
That is on spirits, though, the minister says?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The increase I have given is on spirits. It is very small; I do not know what percentage it is.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: What is the increase on beer?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Eighteen to twenty per cent.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: In volume?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, in volume. The hon. gentleman asks whether this twenty per cent increase in the duty on malt will cause an increase in the price of beer. There are some indications, I am informed, that the breweries may absorb the increased tax, but I do not know about that. The brewers .might absorb the increased- tax, but I do not know. They will probably find some way of passing it on.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The minister cannot tell me what the increased tax would be spread over a case?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, I cannot give that. I do not know what policy the brewers will pursue.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Assuming they passed it on, would there be figures available for that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It would be roughly ten
cents a case.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: There is no legal or economic reason why the brewers should absorb it unless they feel that it is so small they would not want to raise the price to their customers, the taverns and so on. Does the minister not think that an increased tax on malt and all the other ingredients which results in an increase in the price of beer of only ten cents a case is a very moderate contribution to the war effort on the part of those who drink beer?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is the increase.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I know,
but it is no increase at all to the consumer if the brewers absorb it. It does occur to me that here is a field which the minister can usefully explore to add something to the war effort of the country, and I suggest that he had better reconsider the matter. Ten cents a case on beer is a mere bagatelle.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There has been an increase of 100 per cent since the war. It was 6 cents per pound before the war and it was raised to 10 cents in September, 1939, and now 12 cents. We have doubled it.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Yes, and the minister has doubled the taxes on other things. But has he gone the limit on this to-day? I am suggesting that on these items, malt, malt syrup and all the rest of the ingredients that are raw material for the brewer, there is not enough being paid under the circumstances, having regard to the fact that a war is on.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
On April 29, the day he delivered the budget speech, the minister wrote to each provincial premier with respect to income and corporation tax. A copy of that letter was brought down on May 9 in response to a motion dated May 5, as follows:
For a copy of the letter addressed by the Minister of Finance to each provincial premier asking that the provinces should vacate the personal income tax and the corporation tax fields.
The letter was as follows:
Ottawa, April 29, 1941.
Dear Sir:
To-day I sent you a telegram of which the following is a copy:
"In budget speech to-day I will on behalf of government of Canada make an offer to the government of each province in respect of provincial and dominion revenues for duration of war. I am writing you sending you a copy of my speech which contains particulars of offer and shall be pleased to discuss proposal with you at your convenience."
I am enclosing a copy of my budget speech, which contains the offer to which I referred in my telegram, fully explaining the proposal and the reasons why the government of Canada felt it necessary to make it.
I shall be glad to discuss this matter with you at any time at your convenience^ after you have had an opportunity of considering it.
Yours very truly,
(Original signed by J. L. Ilsley.)
Was this the first intimation the provinces had received, other than the suggestion at the time of the dominion-provincial conference -or threat; I do not know which designation the minister would apply to it, but I prefer "suggestion"-that the government would have to invade the provincial field? If so, why did the government not move before the legislatures had all adjourned, so that the provinces could adjust themselves to the new conditions? What has been the reply from the various provinces? Have they agreed to assist the minister by vacating this field, or what is the position?
In the course of his budget speech the minister made what I thought was a generous offer to the provinces if they should vacate this field; they were given not only one but an alternative proposal. In the remarks I made a week ago to-day I stated, as I do now, that it was a generous offer and I hoped the provinces would comply.
It is now two weeks since the minister made his speech, and I should like to know what the position is with respect to the
provinces. I quite understand that there will be great difficulty in the provinces adjusting themselves to such a proposal now that the legislatures are not in session. Their income taxes and corporation taxes are imposed and collected by virtue of statutes of their own legislatures. To ask them at this time to vacate the field for this year may cause a great deal of dislocation and delay. Yet I hope some accommodation will be arrived at, because I have very strong views on the question of double taxation, taxation by provinces and by dominion, taxation on the same money and taxes on taxes.
I understand that consideration is given in some fields to that last topic. I ask the minister to explain the whole position in respect to this matter, because it is one of very great importance, not only to dominion and provincial treasuries, but even more so to the individual taxpayer -who has to pay the bill. After all we are here representing the taxpayers, not the provincial governments. It is still fair to say that they have to be considered, and their financial position has to be taken into account. What is the situation? How far has the minister got?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman was present when the conference to consider the Sirois report met in this chamber, and I am sure he heard what was said on that occasion. So far as I can recollect, there was no communication with the provinces that had anything to do with the matters that were discussed at that conference, until my budget speech. To that statement there should be this exception made, that we did notify them that we could not go on in this fiscal year with the payment of unemployment relief, that the dominion would discontinue those grants.
The reason the offer to the provinces contained in the budget was not made before was because it was not ready before. It was an offer that had to be carefully considered; and when I say "carefully considered" that is understating the case very greatly. It was an offer that could not be modified once it was made; an offer which, if accepted, would have very far-reaching consequences. It necessitated much research, investigation and knowledge of the corporation taxes in the various provinces, not only the ad valorem taxes but the specific taxes as well. It was an offer that could not lightly be made, and it took some time to prepare. And there was another reason, perhaps. It was an offer that had to be accompanied by definite action on the part of the Canadian government.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
That is, compensating action?
Income War Tax Act

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, definite action in the imposition of taxes. Rightly or wrongly, that seemed to us to be the only course that could be pursued. We tried the conference course in January, without success.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: That was on the basis of the Sirois report, but you did not try it on the basis of an all-out war effort.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: That was exactly the position taken by the Premier of Ontario. He said if the government would confer about these matters on the basis of an all-out war effort, for the duration of the war, they would sit in; but that offer was refused. I have no brief for the province of Ontario, but let us face the facts squarely.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am sorry I have not before me the speech I made on that occasion.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I remember it very well.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Whatever the words of that speech, it was to the effect that we proposed the application of the Sirois report, that we definitely stood by it, and called the conference to discuss the application of that report. I gave the reasons why we were in favour of the adoption of the report. I stated our problems, and I said that unless the conference was prepared to discuss with us the application of the report, the adoption of our solution for it, or present an alternative offer of some kind which would meet those problems, I did not see what was to be gained by going on with the conference. Perhaps those were not exactly the words I used at that time, but certainly I suggested that some alternative suggestion be made. No alternative suggestion was made. The position taken by certain premiers attending that conference was that they would not discuss those problems on the basis of the Sirois report; and as that dealt with the whole field it was impossible to go ahead.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Of course that was founded on the theory that the recommendations of the Sirois report were not for the duration of the war but for all time. But the provinces did definitely offer to discuss some of these problems, perhaps all of them, not on the basis of the Sirois report but on the basis of united effort by the provinces and the dominion. That offer was not even considered; it was refused out of hand, and I think that showed a great lack of national leadership on the part of the federal government. I have not the least doubt about that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman is
entitled to his opinion, but I think plenty of leadership has been shown here. I believe that is also the opinion of the country.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Well, I am not so sure of that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. gentleman asked me what is the present position. The present position is that I have heard from all the provinces with the exception [DOT] of Ontario. I have had no indication from Ontario as to whether that province will or will not accept the offer I made.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: British Columbia stated that it was prepared to accept the offer in principle; and while I have not heard anything very definite from the other provinces, because I have not asked for anything very definite, the attitude is an acceptance in principle by most of them, if not all. You will understand, Mr. Chairman, that a province is in a somewhat difficult position with regard to saying "I accept that offer." The premier or provincial treasurer, or both, come to Ottawa or communicate with Ottawa and ask many questions. They say, "If we do this, what will you do?" They ask what this means, what that means; from what date will it start; what arrangements will be made with regard to arrears, and so on. They have a hundred questions.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: They are exploring the whole position.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition

That is
very zeasonable.

speechtext: I should say that all the provinces are now exploring the position, with a disposition to accept the offer, with the exception of Ontario, from which I have not heard.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Are the replies, if they may be termed such, from the various provinces in writing? Take British Columbia, for example; have they put anything in writing in reply to the invitation which was extended on April 29, or has it all been verbal? Has any conclusion been reached in any case? I rather gather from what the minister has said that in no case -has a conclusion been reached?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
It was
interesting to learn from the minister, Mr. Chairman, that he has had no reply -from Ontario. I do not think we should infer from

Income War Tax Act
that silence that there will be no reply; I should think that courtesy at least would require that a reply be given, and that in due course the minister will hear from Ontario. But this appears to be a very important matter to the treasury of Ontario. If my recollection serves me aright, nearly half the entire income tax receipts under present legislation comes from Ontario. I have not the figures in mind at the moment, but undoubtedly the minister knows them. The percentage is very large, and for that reason the subject matter is of great importance not only to the government of Ontario but also to the people of this province. Until some accommodation has been reached between the government of Ontario and this government, does the minister propose to go ahead and place the taxpayers of Ontario in the position that they will have to pay a greatly increased income tax from now on? 1 do suggest to the minister that this would be a very bad situation. I do not wish anything I may say this afternoon to be taken as adding fuel to any flame that now may be burning in that respect. I have views on this subject; I expressed them on the budget. I think it would be wholly regrettable if an accommodation should not be reached; I say this on behalf of the taxpayers of the country. I would much rather see one income tax levied throughout the country than two or three. There may not be any relief in the volume of the tax, but there should be uniformity. I have the hope that there will be some saving in the cost of collection and administration.
In connection with the corporation tax, I had hoped that we would get this thing cleaned up, not only for the duration of the war but for all time. The way this corporation tax is inflicted-that is a good word to use in connection with my province-is beyond all reason. In that province it is imposed, not only on profits but on the capital structure of the corporation. If a corporation is not making any money, and there are still some that are not, the tax must be paid on the basis of the capital structure and to that extent the capital structure is impaired. That is a bad situation. I had hoped that if the provinces give up this field of corporation tax, a great inequity would be done away with. I have much more faith in the equity of dominion taxation than I have in that of the provinces. Many of the provincial taxes have grown up like Topsy. They have seized something here and something there in an effort to get more money. I am speaking particularly of the smaller provinces.
The tax upon public utilities is inequitable. The government has imposed a tax upon long
distance telephone messages with the idea, and properly so, that this tax will be passed on to the consumer or the customer. The government of New Brunswick imposes a tax upon the telephone company, a public utility, and has expressly forbidden any part of it being passed on to the customer. What has been the result? It has had to come out of the shareholders. They have not attempted to do what I think they ought to do, namely, go to the public utility commission and ask for an increase in rates to cover these increased taxes. The result so far has been a reduction in the dividend rates.

Is that not a matter for
the provincial government rather than for the dominion government?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition

I am

I am afraid that there will not be much relief because the increase in the income tax which will be paid by this particular class of company is so great that dividends will have to be impaired. If hon. members want to see the effect of this legislation all they have to do is to look at the quotations of Bell Telephone shares. People's capital has been wiped out indirectly because of the greatly increased taxation. The shares of this company have fallen below 140. The company has been paying eight per cent, but it is not known whether that rate can be maintained. Most of the stock was purchased at a cost of 150. I suggest to the minister that he ought to consider how far and how fast he intends to go with these income tax proposals, especially in the absence of any agreement with Ontario, which in the end will pay a large portion of the whole bill. Does he intend to go on or not?

I am pleased that the dominion is taking over the field of income taxation, and I hope it will be possible to come to some arrangement with the provinces whereby this will be continued. I am also glad that it is entering the field of death duties. I do not agree with some of the remarks made by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) in connection with the recent conference on the Sirois report. I was here at the time and I do think that the Prime Minister (Air. Mackenzie King) should have given a more definite lead to the conference. I was under the impression that any problem having to do with the economy of Canada could be discussed under the report of the Rowell-Sirois commission. While I did not agree with all the recommendations made by the commission, I thought it most regrettable that the conference did not proceed.
As one who represents a Saskatchewan constituency, I am glad that the budget included a provision under which the dominion would service the provincial debt if the province would vacate the income tax field. I think that will be of material help to my province.
Can the minister give us a break-down of the money collected from the various divisions of taxpayers in the dominion, say for the last fiscal year or the year before? 1 have before me some figures which appeared in the Manitoba Free Press of May 7 and which purported to come from the bureau of statistics. I have not had time to check these with the bureau, but as a rule I find that any statistics given by the representative of the Manitoba Free Press who reports the proceedings of this house are accurate. I am accepting them on that basis. The figures are as follows:

I do not think anyone in this country is going to complain about the income tax which is levied to enable us to carry out our part in this war, but I do suggest that we are reaching down lower than I think we ought to reach with our national defence tax. The question to my mind is not how much the taxpayer pays, but how much is left after the taxes are paid. Income tax is the fairest form of taxation, and for the purposes for which we are raising money now it is the best form of taxation; but there is a feeling across the country that wealth is being concentrated more and more, and that since the war broke out large accumulations of wealth have been encouraged. I have never been able to find any figures to substantiate the statement, but I have been told that since the war broke out something like twenty new millionaires have been created.
Let us have the facts.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I should like to know where they are.
I said that I have not been able to find any figures to substantiate the statement.
Has the hon. member been able to find one of these new millionaires?

I have no millionaires in my circle of friends or acquaintances, and so I cannot answer the question from personal knowledge. But statistics brought down in the way I have mentioned lend themselves to that type of criticism and to that kind of interpretation. Our people have the right to know exactly what the social results of the large expenditures for our war effort are, and how government expenditure and taxation affect various classes of people. Consequently I ask the minister if he can give us a breakdown of the income tax divisions for 1940, we will say; and I ask him in giving the figures not to stop at $10,000 and then simply say, "above $10,000 there are no individual figures but the aggregate income is $200,000,000." To-day we are raising taxation on a graduated scale, with categories of taxpayers with incomes ranging from less than $1,000 right up to $1,000,000, and in my opinion the time has come when there should be given a break-

down of incomes or of the income taxes covering as many of these classifications as it is possible to include at this time. I realize, of course, that our graduated scale up to the present has not been in this form, but it has been in a form which would enable the department to give the committee a better breakdown than the one to which I referred, which as I say I got from the Manitoba Free Press a day or two ago.
We are often asked as to the accumulation of wealth in the hands of a few people in Canada, and I think it would be well for this house and the country to know whether or not the statements which are sometimes made are really based on the facts.
When we are discussing the schedules of taxation we should keep in mind that it is not what the taxpayer pays but the amount which the taxpayer has left that really counts. In the national defence tax and income tax we are reaching down into very low income brackets. In my opinion we are taking too much from the lower brackets. I believe all our people should make a contribution to the war effort, but their contributions should be based on something which is fair, equitable and just. It is for this reason that I ask that
the information I have requested be given before we proceed with further consideration of the schedules.

speechtext: The mere statement of income itself does not carry with it the argument that income is based on invested capital. It may be, and perhaps largely is, based on services rendered, which is quite a different thing.

In calculating income tax
of those serving in the militia and in the naval and air forces, including private soldiers, is any other income he may have taken into account?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Besides his service pay?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Private soldiers and noncommissioned officers in the Canadian active service forces are not taxable, either for national defence tax or in respect of service pay and allowances. They are taxable on other income. Officers are not taxable on the pay and allowances which they receive while overseas or which they receive while

they are in a position the duties of which normally take them on the sea or in the air. I am not stating it exactly in the words of the statute, but that is substantially what the law is. But officers in the Canadian active service forces whose duties do not normally take them on the sea or in th< air and who are not overseas-that is, officers, here in Canada, with exceptions I have mentioned-pay income tax and national defence tax on service pay and allowances as well as on other income.

I suggest the advisability of exempting officers as well as men in the militia and in the naval and air forces. Commissioned officers, while they may receive a reasonable rate of pay, have heavy obligations in many respects. They must procure uniforms if they are to look the splendid, well-groomed officers they are, and they have social as well as family obligations. I cannot help thinking that the men who are now in the service here but not on the high seas or participating in actual engagements are nevertheless not in any stay-at-home army. They are in the fight to the finish as we all are.
Those of us who watched the men returning from the last great war saw at that time, after four years of desperate conflict, officers coming back who were aged and worn by their service, and they returned to new fields of business activity. It does seem to me that in the period following this war, which now promises to be longer than the last one, men who are now old enough to become commissioned officers will have missed the opportunity to take prominent places in the business life of the country. Their earning capacity will have disappeared. Many of our commissioned officers of to-day are keen business and professional men. In many instances when they enlisted they gave up excellent possibilities. When they return they will find their places taken by those who have risen in the business ranks, by those who have benefited by increased pay in the interim. The war is bearing heavily upon all classes of taxpayers, down into the small brackets, affecting homes that have never heretofore known what income tax was. I realize that the minister is faced with a gigantic problem if he is to meet the obligations that fall upon a comparatively small population such as ours. I have every sympathy for the government, and I have sympathy for the taxpayers of Canada, especially those in the small brackets. The man with $50,000 a year income who has to pay $20,000 or $30,000 is not as hard hit as the man with a very small salary. But the soldier is in an entirely different position. When he returns

Income War Tax Act
after a long war lie will find probably that his possibilities of future advancement have vanished. Many of our commissioned officers are forty, forty-five and fifty, many are thirty, or thirty-five. When they come back after years of warfare they will have lost touch with the business activities of the country; they will be older army officers.
There is not an, hon. member who cannot recall the days after the last war when men came back and could not find places. I know of excellent men who were more or less out of a job from one war to the other. I suggest that the minister might well consider exemption for all. He has stated that he will exempt those on the high seas. Why make two bites at the cherry? I realize that he needs money, but the amount involved is not very large. I suggest that at least it might be set aside as a form of pension for these men. Even the man in the factory whose hourly rates of pay -have been increased has gained advantages, from increased number of hours and- consequent increase in remuneration, over the SI.30 a day which the private receives. I know he is not objecting to paying a reasonable tax on- the higher wages he will have, but besides receiving higher wages he has the possibility of retaining a job through the years. He has the possibility of advancement in his company through the ability and industry he may show.
When this war ends, thousands of men who come back will not find the place in business that should properly be theirs by reason1 of the ability they demonstrated before they left, or, no doubt, are demonstrating as officers. It appears to me that we might well give them consideration, and I urge it upon the government. I did not take the time of the house during the debate; I realized then that there was no amendment offered by my leader, but I have felt for some time -that we should give serious consideration to exempting all soldiers from income tax on their income received in the service, whether military, naval or air force. In addition, I might draw to the attention of the minister the danger these men face as they go overseas; these men are enlisting for service not so much here -in Canada as where the fighting is. We are building a fighting force; we are not building a stay-at-home army in this conflict which is now developing into a battle to -the death. These men are ready to sacrifice their lives as well as to lose their -opportunities. They must dress neatly and preserve the dignity of the Canadian Army; they have their social responsibilities; and with -the slightly increased salary, if they have some left I think it might be added to their capital for the rain3' 14873-1754
day that so often follows for an older army officer. I plead with the government to reconsider the tax on soldiers' incomes.

I -would impress upon the minister something that goes part way along the road with my hon. friend who has just resumed his seat, namely, with reference to officers whose only income is their service pay. One can conceive that a gallant -man who had a substantial private income as an officer might not need or even desire exemption with regard to his military pay. But for an officer who abandons everything else and has no income other than that which he receives as an officer, I suggest that it should be exempt.

If the hon. member will pardon my interruption I believe we are more or less in accord, but I think he misunderstood my statement. I am only proposing exemption on what they earn as pay. For instance, if an officer had a large income apart from his pay I do not mean that that should be exempt.

I so understood the hon. member, but my proposal is not quite that.
With regard to the point raised by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, that there should be a break-down of incomes of $50,000 or over, which are now included in one item, personally I cannot see any public interest that is served by not furnishing that break-down. The work would not be too onerous, and in the present mental attitude of the people with regard to seeing that those best able to pay bear the greatest burden, it would be a healthy thing to have added to the schedule which will appear on Hansard a further break-down of incomes of $50,000 and over, perhaps in brackets jumping $20,000 at a time.
One other suggestion I have, which perhaps is not feasible this year, is that instructions should be given to the commissioner of income tax-I think I can say our expert and worthy commissioner to whom this country is indebted, Mr. Elliott-that next year in connection with the break-down which will be given to parliament on this subject, earned income should be shown separately from investment income. In other words, when we get this statement next year there should be a breakdown of the total incomes in two columns, showing what portion of those incomes is earned and what portion accrues from investments. It is a good principle that this budget enunciates as I understand it, namely, that it discriminates to some extent between earned income and investment income. If I read the signs aright, the temper of the people, it will be that as we proceed with perhaps heavier war burdens in future, a greater burden should be placed upon unearned or investment incomes than on incomes which are earned.
Income War Tax Act

The government should exercise extreme care with regard to taxing the money which this country pays to the men of the fighting forces. I raised this question before in connection with the transportation tax; it applies to a large extent with regard to income tax as well. It seems to me that the principle of asking a man to fight, paying him, and then taxing that pay, ought to be carefully reviewed. I should like to associate myself in general principle with many of the views which have here been expressed.
My main reason, however, for rising this afternoon is to bring to the attention of the minister and the committee something by way of renewal of a matter which I and other hon. members raised at a previous session, and I think mention was also made of it this session in connection with the debate on going into committee of ways and means, namely, the matter of exemptions under the income tax act.
Hon. members will recall that when we met at the first session of this parliament, in 1940, there was quite a strenuous plea to extend the exemption to those of our taxpayers who were accommodating in their homes children evacuated from Britain. The minister and the government in their wisdom decided to limit the exemptions to those having children who were evacuated under the cooperative scheme sponsored by the governments of Canada and the United Kingdom, or of any of the provinces of Canada. Answering a question in the house on November 20, 1940, the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Crerar) indicated that up to that date we had in Canada from Great Britain 1,532 guest children under the cooperative evacuation scheme. In addition to that, however, and outside of the government plans we had 4,326 children brought into private homes.
I think this is a fair principle to enunciate; I think it would be a fair principle for the government to adopt. If we have citizens of this country who are ready and willing to spend their money in what is perhaps one of the most important of our patriotic causes; If they are actually contributing in this way to our war effort-for this is really part and parcel of that effort-then I do not think it is asking too much to request that the minister seriously consider extending these exemptions to that extent.	_
We have an excellent example to guide us in this matter. Since the last session of this house the Ontario government has dealt with this subject; and of course the principles of the income tax legislation of the dominion and that of the province are very similar, except for changes in phraseology which are brought about by the fact that the one is the

dominion and the other is the province. The provincial income tax amendments brought down by the attorney general were further amended by the government before being put through the legislature; and I wish to commend to the minister the amendment adopted by Ontario in this regard. The section to which I have reference reads as follows:
Subsection 1 of section 5 of the Income Tax Act (Ontario) as amended by section 1 of the Income Tax Amendment Act, 1939, and section 3 of the Income Tax Amendment Act, 1940, is further amended by adding thereto the following paragraph:
(ee) Four hundred dollars for each child evacuated during the present war from the United Kingdom of Great Britain, Ireland or the British dominions beyond the seas under twenty-one years of age and dependent upon the taxpayer for support and maintained by the taxpayer in Ontario; provided that the tax reduction obtained as a result of such deduction shall not in any case exceed the amount of tax reduction which would be received by a married person without dependents in respect of an income of five thousand dollars.
I bring this to the attention of the minister and the committee as an indication of what another legislative body in this country has done in dealing with this question. I feel strongly about this matter; it does seem unfair to make a distinction between the two classes of children, because it costs about the same to maintain a child no matter under what scheme it may have been brought to this country. In the case of a child brought out under a private arrangement, the parents in England, because of exchange regulations, are not permitted to contribute anything to its support; the whole burden falls on the Canadian guardians, and I do not see the justification for the definite distinction that has been drawn between children brought here under the government scheme and those brought out privately.
I should like the minister, if possible, to give some consideration to this suggestion. I know there is a widespread feeling among many classes of our citizens that this taxation contains an element of injustice and unfairness, which I think should not be permitted to continue.

Would the minister elaborate on the statement he made as to the number of individual taxpayers and the amount of the tax collected? When he makes up the statement he is going to place on Hansard, would he include the estimated tax increases for 1941 and also the estimated increases that will be brought about by the new taxes, which will be collected after March 31 next, in the categories set out in this table? We have all the other information,

and I think it would be interesting and illuminating to have the increases in the various categories.

Yes, the increases
by income groups.

Has the minister
not an estimate made up?

Would the minister be prepared to make a statement with regard to exemptions in respect of these guest children? I know several instances where people have had young relatives sent out to them, and it is a serious matter for them. They are people of modest means, and the exemption would mean a great deal to them. I do not believe the present provision is wide enough to meet the requirements; and also, as I understand it, no exemption at all is provided in respect of the national defence tax. Is that correct?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That will be changed. I
have an amendment in that regard.

While most hon. members
appear to be in sympathy with the suggestion that has been made, I would point out that in many instances people expect and are looking for payment, if not now at least when the war is over. In many instances such payment is simply deferred. I know that most of the people with whom I have come in contact never had in mind asking for or receiving any exemption at all; they did this as a grand gesture, without thought of reward. I would suggest that the minister should be careful not to make this exemption too wide, because I am sure many of these people expect to be fully paid after the war is over.
In reply to that statement, if anyone feels that he does not wish to take advantage of the exemption he can simply ignore that part of the form when he fills out his income tax return.

I should like to direct the minister's attention to a slightly different angle of this income tax question. I am speaking as one who recently paid income tax for the first time; and under the new rates I shall have to pay twice as much in the coming year. I am not making any complaint. People with small incomes, who find that this
year their income taxes will be doubled, are doing only what they expected to do in this emergency. In the table which appears at page 2348 of Hansard I notice these rates in the low income group:
