Going down the list, however, I find that those with large incomes still will be left with what I consider altogether too much for any family.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
They are being increased
more in proportion, though.
That is not the point. As the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar said, the point is not how much income tax you pay but rather how much you have left after you pay your income tax.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If I may ask a question,
is that argument not based upon the theory that the net income remaining to all the people in the country should be equal?

No, not necessarily.
I should like to deal with that. According to this table, an individual with an income of S50,000, which makes the salary of the minister seem like small change, will pay $26,965 under the proposed rates. But how much has he left? He has still left $23,035. These figures are so large that they do not mean anything. In order to reduce them to terms which I could understand, I calculated on the basis of six days a week, fifty weeks in the year, which gave me three hundred days. After an individual with an income of $50,000 pays his income tax on the new scale, he will still have left $76.78 a day. An individual with an income of $75,000 will have to pay a tax of $43,935, but he will still have left $103.55 a day. An individual with an income of $100,000 will pay under the new plan a tax of $61,875, but he will have left $127.08 a day. An individual with an income of $150,000 will have left $166.95 a day after paying his new tax. An individual with an income of $200,000 will have left $202.43 a day. An individual with an income of $500,000 will have left $329.60 a day.
I am not one of those who assume that even if you took the entire income of the 483 individuals who reported incomes of $50,000 a year you would solve the problem of financing the war, but I contend that if you took a larger amount from those who can afford to contribute you would be making a valuable contribution toward strengthening the morale of the Canadian people. Those with
Income War Tax Act

lower incomes are finding that the cost of living is increasing. They are being compelled to support national war savings campaigns; they cannot turn down these appeals, and they find it difficult to balance their budgets. I submit that those with really large incomes can pay a larger tax without seriously reducing their standards of living. While the minister has made some increases, I do not think he has gone far enough in increasing the tax upon incomes of 850,000 and over.

I find myself largely in
agreement with the remarks of the last speaker, but I certainly would not take this stand in peace time. In war time we have an entirely different situation. The aim in war time is to reduce spending in order to divert materials to our war needs. Therefore, I feel that everyone should be prepared to have his income cut down to a point where he is just able to maintain a decent standard of living. A man should not expect during war time to be able to save large amounts of money which, as I have often remarked, really represent to a large degree profits made from the war. The sale of bonds will have to come from exactly the saime place as the taxation. If we put into execution what I would term a reasonable scale of taxation for war time, the people would not have money with which to buy bonds. I would be quite prepared to increase considerably the taxation upon the higher salaries, say down to the level of $3,000 or $4,000, so that people will have just enough to maintain a decent standard of living. Then it would not be necessary to sell bonds. That is why I opposed the proposition of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation that we should institute compulsory loans. If we had a proper scale of taxation there would be no money left with which to buy bonds. If people invest their incomes in war bonds, even though those bonds do not bear interest, at the end of the war they will have a claim against future production. That will be a claim against production representing profits made out of the war. I quite agree with the last speaker when he says that higher incomes should be taxed still further.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not know how far a discussion like this is likely to be fruitful. As I understand the position taken by the last hon. gentleman, it is that we should take everything from people except just enough to live on. If I understand their proposition correctly, that amount would be equal for all people.
Not necessarily.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If it is not to be equal for everyone, then that is just what we have done now. We have taken a large proportion of the income of these people.
Not from the people with large incomes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: An increasingly large amount. Most people earn small incomes. I have never had a very large income, and I find it difficult to see what a person could do with an income of $50,000. I would not know how to spend it, and I do not know just how they spend it. It is often considered an injustice that a lawyer is able to earn $500 a day in court. But not very far from him in the same city or town may be lawyers who are on relief. They had the same chance as the man who is able to earn $500 a day in court to get themselves into that position, but because they did not have the ability or the industry or the character, they were not able to.
Not all lawyers get in that position.
Would the hon. member like them to?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There are some people who, because of their application, industry and character, because of a certain firmness or determination, because of some other qualities which may or may not be admirable, have got themselves into a position where they are able to earn high incomes. When they do, they are likely to buy larger houses, have more extensive grounds around them, have many pieces of fine furniture, and so on. Suppose we come along and do as the hon. gentleman has suggested we should, take everything above $3,000 or $4,000. That would mean wholesale liquidation of property and a complete upset in the standards of living and the arrangements which have been established. I am not at all sure that that would be in the interests of the community. In fact, I am sure that a sudden inroad upon established arrangements of society would create so much dislocation that it would do more harm than good to our war effort. In imposing taxation of this kind some regard must be had for the manner of life in the country. In countries like England, the United States and Canada, the higher taxes imposed are proportionate to the other taxes. For instance, this year the increases in the taxes on the higher incomes have been greater proportionately-

The percentage of
increase?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No; I see what the hon. member has in mind. We gave a great deal of thought to what would be a fair graduation

Income War Tax Act
of increases. If you have a ten per cent rate on a lower income and a sixty per cent rate on a higher income, when you double the ten per cent rate you cannot double the sixty per cent rate. You cannot make a proportionate increase like that. We took the amount of income that they had left after the payment of the taxes heretofore existing, that is the taxes for the year 1940-41, and the increase in taxes for the low income man would be, let us say, five per cent. For the man with a higher income tax levy, the increase would be six per cent of the amount levied. For the man with a higher income the proportion of that increase to the amount levied was a higher rate. You will find a complete graduation right through, and the proportion which the increase in taxation bears to the amount of income which the taxpayers have left rises progressively throughout the whole range. That is how we have graduated our increases, and I think it is the fair way.

Will the minister make a
statement about guest children?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes; I made a statement
last year on that. I know there are quite a number of members in this house and quite a number of people in the country who can see only one side of this question and who think the government should contribute to the maintenance of these guest children in this manner, because that is what it amounts to. I gave the reasons very fully last year, and I do not think I need repeat them; but I wish to point out that if we are going to get away from status as a test of whether a deduction from income is to be allowed for dependents, we must stop somewhere, and if we are going to take the praiseworthiness of the foster parents as a test, or dependency without any relationship, without even legal relationship such as adoption, we should be going into a very wide field.
Oh, no.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Oh, yes. I have received
only one letter from a member of parliament, not more, who pointed out that he had advocated in this house for years a deduction in respect of foster children, Canadians, taken into homes in this country. I have made inquiries to find how many instances of that kind there are, and I believe there is no record of it. Whether the census of 1931 would give it, I do not know. I am told, however, that in some parts of Canada there are large numbers of foster children. People take into their homes a young niece or a nephew, or some other relation; but we have refused consistently, as I said to the house last year, to permit a deduction in respect of
foster children, and I would not feel like agreeing to a deduction on behalf of guest children unless I was prepared to go further and permit a deduction to taxpayers who take in foster children, relatives of theirs, and others, without any adoption at all. I am not prepared to do that because we would run into a great variety of circumstances necessitating investigation as to whether there was real dependency, and so we have left the matter as it is, permitting a deduction when the child is the taxpayer's own child, either natural or by adoption. It sounds easy to say, adopt this proposal with respect to guest children. But somebody said there were something like five thousand guest children in this country; I think it was the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon).
The number is 4,326.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Let us say 5,000 for the
sake of making the figure even. If all the taxpayers who have guest children in their homes were paying on an income of $5,000, it would work out to $144 a child. That means a contribution out of the treasury of Canada of 5,000 multiplied by $144. But let us suppose that that is too high and that the average would be $100. That would be 5,000 multiplied by $100, which would be $500,000 out of the treasury of Canada. Hon. gentlemen can think the matter over for themselves. I ask them, do they think we should accept such a proposal at a time like this when we are taxing our low-paid girls working in department stores and our workmen on low incomes and other low-paid workers everywhere? We have to put heavy taxes on the low-paid people because the numbers are there and the additional wealth to a great extent is going there. At a time like that, are we to make a contribution out of the treasury of Canada of something like $100 for a child who has been brought here, not at the instance of the government at all, but by people who have taken these children out of their own generosity? Are we to come along and make a contribution such as I have indicated? I have every admiration for these people who take in these children, but they started to be generous themselves, and I think it is well enough for the government to leave it to them to handle the situation themselves. If it were a government-sponsored scheme, that would be a different situation entirely. It may be, I will admit, pretty hard to draw the line between cases, but it is not going to be half so hard as to draw the line between guest children and the rest, of

Income War Tax Act
the children who are in homes all over Canada but who are no relation to their foster parents. I do not know how big a drain on the treasury it would be if we had to do that

If the minister will permit a question-I do not wish to interrupt him- the taxpayers of this country are allowed exemption on the contributions they make to funds for war victims overseas and various other patriotic funds. Does the minister think it fair to exempt such contributions and not to exempt the children who have come here from overseas? A man wishes to adopt a guest child, but some other family gets that child, and so the first man contributes instead, S500, we will say, to a war victims or war services fund, and his contribution is exempt from taxation. Does the minister think it is fair to exempt such contributions and not to make an allowance for the guest children?
Personally I do not think there is any comparison at all, because people are taking these guest children as a war effort, and many of the poorer parents in Great Britain will not be able to pay for the care of their children here after the war. Many of us in this house have tried to secure guest children but did not secure them, and if we do our duty we should, instead, contribute as much as we feel we can to some war services fund. The department allows us exemption for anything we contribute to these war services funds, and I think that is sound.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No; let me straighten my hon. friend out on that. As a general principle, no deduction on account of gifts to private charities is permitted.
It is the same thing.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am answering the hon.
gentleman, who said that if we give money for this purpose and that purpose, an exemption is allowed. When we give to public charities, a deduction of gifts to such charitable organizations is permitted, with one exception to which I shall refer, but only up to ten per cent of the taxpayer's net taxable income. The exception to that is the exception provided in the War Charities Act, under which donations to charitable organizations were permitted up to fifty per cent of the taxpayer's net taxable income, provided that these charities were approved by the government through the Secretary of State. Under that provision, charities such as the Red Cross and other approved charities-there were only six of them altogether-made their appeals, and taxpayers' donations were permitted as a deduction from income for income tax purposes up to fifty per cent. But we had so much
fMr. Ilsley.]
trouble with that and so much complaint of discrimination as between patriotic and nonpatriotic charities that we had to discontinue it, and I am proposing an amendment to that effect, of which I made announcement to the house in my budget speech. The national war services drive, however, was getting under way. The Red Cross had had the benefit of two appeals on the fifty per cent basis, and it was felt that the other organizations should be permitted their second appeal on the same basis. I agreed to a modification, but that provision was to terminate and apply only to subscriptions up to April 7, provided they were paid before December 31. But now the bars are up. I am not doing the whole thing myself because I am going to ask the house to agree with me in doing it.
So there will be no exemptions then?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Exemptions only up to ten per cent. You cannot have one rule for the public charities which are doing such a tremendous work in the cities and towns of this country, and another rule for patriotic charities. I do not think it has any bearing on these private charities if I give money, if I take a child in my home. Canadians have been doing it since confederation, since there has been an income tax act, and they never got any exemption at all.
We did not have this income tax in the old days.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They did not get an exemption in respect of these children unless they made them their own children.

At that time the Minister of Finance was not such an intruder in the homes of the people of Canada, and his demands did not affect so largely the incomes of the people. The situation which the minister has outlined is simply this: he says that these people who have very kindly taken in guest children from the old country invited them of their own free will to come to their own homes. But they did so with the idea that the income which they had to spend was a certain amount. Since then, income taxes have been raised very substantially, not once, but twice, so that a larger part of the family income is going to the Department of National Revenue. This makes it extremely difficult for them to carry on. I do not see, Mr. Chairman, that any amount of logic will rectify the injustice which the failure of the government to allow this exemption perpetrates.

Income War Tax Act
I should like to ask the minister why it is that the Department of National Revenue is not willing to grant the exemption for children to any person who looks after children in this country, whether or not that particular person happens to be the parent. I do not see why, if one's sister dies, her husband having predeceased her, and the brother looks after the children so that they will not become a public charge, that brother should not be granted relief in so far as exemption for those children is concerned. I put a question on the order paper after the minister had given his answer in the last budget debate, and the reply I got from the Prime Minister was. nil. The question went something like this, "How many foster children are there in the Dominion of Canada, and how many of these are related by blood or marriage to the foster parent?" The answer given to me was that a census would have to be taken to get this information, and the Prime Minister smiled, as if it were a semi-foolish question. But I pointed out to him that government policy was being based on the answer to this question; and the Minister of Finance has just said that the policy of not granting exemptions to any people except the actual parents of the children is a well-defined and well-settled policy, resting on something substantial. It is not resting on anything at all substantial that I can see. You do not know how many foster children there are in the country; you simply say that it might open a door and do away with a certain amount of revenue, and you refuse to grant exemptions in respect of these refugee children because you might have to grant exemptions on behalf of certain other children. I can see no basis for the decision. You have to raise money, but there is no reason why you must commit an injustice.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I will go this far with the hon. gentleman: I think that where the government has to take charge of a child brought out by private arrangement and put it in another home, consideration should be given to those cases by the Department of National Revenue.
I think that has been done.

It seems to me an
invidious distinction.

May I point out to the minister that apparently he has two lines of defence in this question: one, relating to the evacuated child who is in a private home; and the other, the foster child; yet in Ontario no such difficulty as he has suggested appears to have arisen in the minds of the legislators who were dealing with exactly the same problem. The situation as regards the dominion is that they say they can make no exemption for British children who came out under private auspices; but the fact is that those who have taken these children, when they are making out their income tax forms, if Ontario is to continue in the income tax field, are still going to be allowed exemption by the province on entirely the opposite principle, so far as British children are concerned. It

Income War Tax Act

does not seem to me that this indicates any uniformity of legislation as regards the situation created by the evacuation of these children.
I suggest that we could get over the matter in this way. If there is a possible difficulty in distinguishing between foster children and those evacuated under war-time conditions, why could not the amount which the taxpayer pays for the upkeep of the child from the British home, instead of being put under exemptions for children, be deducted as a contribution in the same manner as is done with the Canadian war sendees fund? That would get over all the difficulties so far as foster children are concerned. The minister's second line of defence would then be gone, and the maximum claim could be set at not more than $400. I suggest that that would fully meet the situation and avoid the difficulty of distinguishing between foster children and the others.

I should like to say a word on the question of guest children. In the city of Victoria there is a large population of people from the old country. Many of them brought children into Canada just, about the time the war broke out. They now find themselves in an embarrassing financial position; funds coming from the old country have been stopped, but the children are here and they must be looked after. These people are struggling as best they can; they have in some instances asked their friends to take the children in and look after them, and I think those who do so are entitled to some consideration so far as exemption from income tax is concerned. If the hon. member who has just spoken wants an opportunity to assist in the care of guest children in Canada, we can give him that opportunity,
Income War Tax Act

because we have a school with two hundred in it at the present time. We have room for another fifty, but we have not the funds to bring them out and take care of them. The hon. member for Yale is one of the directors of that school with me, and I am sure we would be glad of a little extra cash to help it along.
I hope the minister will take what has been said to-day seriously and give some relief to those who are at the present time looking after guest children.

A short time ago I
addressed a question to the Minister of Finance as to why the government adopted the policy of not granting to foster parents of children in Canada, whether British evacuees or not, the ordinary exemption for children. It is not clear to me why there should be this discrimination between natural children and children who, while not legally adopted, are nevertheless a charge on a man's income.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is in the nature of private charity. I get letters from sisters looking after a sick sister, who think it unfair that they should not be allowed to deduct something on that account. In all relationships of life situations arise where there is a drain upon the income of certain persons for some generous private charitable purpose. Such instances have never been recognized. The hon. member asks, why are they not recognized? Because claims would be made from the Atlantic to the Pacific; there would be no end of checking necessary; there would be a great drain on the revenue, and it would be very difficult to administer. There is no law that there must be a deduction for all kinds of good-natured expenditures from a person's income before he pays his income tax; he is taxed on his income, not on what he has left after he makes certain expenditures.

I quite appreciate that. On the other hand, ever since I have had any understanding of these matters, children, that is natural children, have been the subject of exemption. I presume there are good and sufficient reasons why a parent gets exemption for natural children. I do not know why the government has any objection to someone receiving exemption for every child in Canada. I do not see why,any particular distinction should be made as to whether the child is actually living with the parents or is being kept by someone else. In fact, the obligation is less upon some person other than the parent than upon the parent. I see no reason why every child under sixteen should not be the subject of exemption in the hands of

the person who is making the necessary financial outlay to maintain that child. Why does the government adopt this rigorous policy? I do not see that it has any ground in sociology or in taxation.

I have heard many hon. members prefacing their remarks with sympathy for the minister for this stupendous task which he has in distributing this burden equitably; but another phase of this question has not been brought out-and this surprises me. I refer to the case of children taken into homes which do not enjoy sufficient income even to qualify for the payment of income tax. I know several of them in my own community of Brantford. What is going to be done in those cases? I am prepared to say that if the situation were analysed it would be found that the most charitable homes very often, so far as taking in other people's children is concerned, would be found among that class of people whose income does not reach the income tax level. I think the minister is quite within his rights in bringing that to the attention of the committee. I have a great deal of sympathy for those who are paying income tax, but hon. members will have a hard job getting any sympathy from the average man on the street for those who qualify for the payment of income tax.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Before the committee rises, according to the arrangement made, I should like to suggest to the minister that when we meet next I want to discuss the question of the preservation of the position of the municipalities under the proposed arrangement with the provinces, particularly in relation to those provinces, like New Brunswick, which have no income tax and where there cannot be any compensation for the giving up of that tax. What will be the position there? If I can, I wish to preserve the position of the municipalities, so that if any concession is made to the provinces in respect of the municipalities giving up certain sources of revenue, that concession will be certain to be passed on to the municipalities. I comprehend that there will be some difficulty in connection with those provinces where there is no income tax at present, and I wish to direct the minister's attention to that position now in order that he may think it over in the interval.

What headway has been made in investigations with respect to forest insect infestations? In the province of Quebec, in New Brunswick and to a smaller extent in Nova Scotia I understand that there have been serious infestations of the forests by the spruce sawfly and other insects.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: As has been reported previously, we are rearing large numbers of parasites to attack the spruce sawfly and certain other pests which destroy the forests. These parasites are being developed largely in laboratories at Belleville, Ontario, and they are being released from time to time to attack the sawfly and other pests. The battle against forest insects is going along fairly successfully. I am not in a position to state just to what extent we have been able to destroy these pests, but they are being attacked on the same plan this year as in previous years.
Have these parasites had the effect of controlling the spread of this infestation of the forests of eastern Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: It is naturally impossible to give actual figures in this regard. In the first place there is no way of determining the number of pests that are there to begin with. But it can be stated that these parasites have established themselves in the vicinities where the pests are, and the spread of the infestation has been lessened in recent years compared with what it was some few years ago. That is about the only way in which we can gauge the effectiveness of the plan which is being followed. Our reports are that the parasites are becoming effective, but as yet are not operating to prevent infestation 100 per cent.
Can the minister state definitely whether the infestation is under complete control in any one area where these parasites have been used?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture

speechtext: This particular pest, the sawfly, I am informed, has never been entirely controlled either in this country or elsewhere through the use of parasites, but it has been materially checked in other countries and is being materially checked here. Our hope at least is that through the use of parasites we can still further check the destruction which has been caused by this pest.

speechtext:
The hon. member will realize that much of the work in fighting the pests and of making the examinations and surveys associated with fighting grasshoppers, for example, is summer w'ork, and
that work is carried on by officials some of whom are part-time men. speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture

There is the temporary employee who is called "temporary" because he is only on part time; there is also the temporary employee who is taken on and cannot be considered for permanency until he has been at least six months in the service, but quite often, or at least sometimes, he is not made permanent until he has been on the staff for a number of years. In connection with the latter type, there is a general rule which applies to different departments, but not exactly in the same percentage, nor does it apply in exactly the same percentage all the way through the Department of Agriculture. Certain branches are allowed a higher percentage of permanents than are others; but generally speaking, it is about eighty per cent to twenty per cent; that is, eighty per cent permanents and twenty per cent temporaries, the idea being that we shall not have at any time on the staff more than a certain percentage who are permanent, and others are advanced in order to keep that percentage at about the same level.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: We have had an offer for the Rosthem farm. I think we have had two offers, one at a lower figure, and the second one at a raised figure. We did not at the time feel inclined to accept the price which was offered. We have also had an offer to rent from the same individual who made the two offers to purchase. We have had under consideration a suggestion that the province might wish to take the farm over and operate it on a certain basis. I believe that a decision i3 to be reached this week. The same reason would not justify not answering the question as to the amount which has been offered. What were the two offers?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I have some doubt about making a statement. I do not know whether it is publicly known in that vicinity or not. AVe called for tenders once, and the first bid was on that tender. When was the call for tenders made, how many were sent in, and what was the amount of the highest tender? We are surely entitled to have the information as to the amount of the tender.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
I have not the figures, but my recollection is that the tenders were called for last fall, although I have not the exact date. There was really only one bid. That can be understood. An experimental farm is one which has buildings that are of no use to anyone who wishes to run an

ordinary farm. We did get one bid, but it was not high enough.

Why is there difficulty in finding out what the amount of the bid was? Does the minister propose to call for tenders again?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: We have not given consideration to that, but I should think that if much more time expires we shall have to call for tenders again.

How many acres are there in the farm, and what does the minister consider the actual value of the farm for farming purposes? That is a fair question. I should like to know how many acres there are and whether it is worth the ordinary value of farming land in the district, more or less.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: It is approximately a section of land, which is 640 acres. I should not like to put a price on it. I am not a land expert, and I have not sufficient knowledge of the farm to state personally what ought to be paid for it. I will, however, say this. As minister of the department I will see that the government gets all it can for it. I am somewhat responsible for the stand, in the first place, that $16 an acre was not enough, with the result that a very much larger amount was offered, although we did not accept that either.
What has been the cost of the farm up to the present time, in the purchase of the land, the erection of buildings and other work of that kind?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I am not in a position to state what the original cost was. I understand that it was added to from time to time, and it would be very difficult, for the reasons I gave a few moments ago, to establish anything from the amount of money that has been spent on the land. We have far more housing capacity there than would be required on any farm operated as a farm. We have many more farm buildings than a farmer would find necessary; we have all sorts of trees for purposes of decoration and for experimental purposes in connection with fruit and other things which to the ordinary farmer would not be useful at all. If one added up all the costs of that kind on the farm it would be many times more than one could expect to get for a farm for farming purposes.

What was the reason for closing it? Has it not been found to be worth while to continue operations on that farm, or is it because of other circumstances? What kind of experimental work was being conducted on the farm? Was it in connection with grain or fruit, or in what direction?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
This farm is located right across the road from Seager Wheeler's farm. Seager Wheeler was one of the men who did a great deal of experimental work in connection with different varieties of wheat. As a matter of fact, he was associated, using his own farm as well, with the department for a number of years and had a certain annual payment from the government, so that much experimental work of that kind was done in that community. He and those operating the farm have also experimented extensively in the growing of fruit trees suitable to that north country. In addition, there was some experimentation in connection with live stock, the same as the experimentations that take place on all experimental farms.
Some years ago, beginning in 1912, the agricultural college was opened at Saskatoon, with a farm associated with it, and about 1,600 acres of that farm are operated very much in the same way as the farm is operated at Guelph, with the result that within a comparatively short distance from the Rosthern farm there was being operated by the province a farm that was doing practically the same kind of work as was being carried out on the Rosthern farm, and under conditions somewhat, though not exactly, similar. A few years ago, during the time that Mr. Weir was Minister of Agriculture, another farm was opened at Mel-fort, which is further east. At that time it was considered necessary by the department to have that farm further east. As a result of these two developments, first, the farm at Saskatoon, which was opened by the province
Supply-Agriculture

in conjunction with the agricultural college, and second, the experimental farm which was opened further east in an area which is rather different and further removed from Saskatoon, the department have been attempting for a considerable time to close this farm down. Much of the live stock which was originally on the farm had been moved away before the farm was actually closed down; and we considered that in view of the fact that a war is on; that in any event we desired to close the farm, and that its closing was a means whereby we could cut down some of the expense, it should have been closed last year, and we closed it.
I understand that five of these farms have been closed.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Yes, five.
The difference is only about $400.

speechtext: Can the minister give the committee the terms of lease or the rental basis of the Rosthern farm?

speechtext:
It is not yet leased.

papers?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I have not the exact date, but it was some time during the latter part of last summer. It was advertised in the papers throughout Saskatchewan. I have no hesitation in saying that there were many inquiries from the community itself, from persons right in Rosthern and outside, and there was a considerable agitation to the effect that certain things should be done with the farm, none of which has been done up to the present.
When arriving at a decision not to accept $16 an acre, or in other words, approximately $11,000 for property which I am informed has buildings on it worth more than $30,000-
What does the hon. member mean by "worth"?
*-the minister must have had an independent valuation, otherwise he would not be in a position to turn down an offer of approximately $10,000. What is the amount of the department's valuation?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I cannot say that; I am not a land valuator, but I know that when a certain bid was made by a certain individual for the farm and we refused to accept it and he offered very much more, that was sufficient reason for having turned down the first bid. Probably we are not justified in turning down the second.

I seem to have some difficulty in getting an answer from the minister. Was there an independent valuation of this property? How does this land, comprising the old Rosthern experimental farm, compare in value with adjoining land? Surely the minister has all that information.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: My hon. friend has lived in the vicinity; he knows that anyone who is living on a farm there and has made a home there would not sell his farm for $50 an acre, and he knows at the same time that anyone who wishes to sell a farm cannot sell it for $20 an acre. It is difficult to sell a farm anywhere in Saskatchewan to-day at $20 an acre if one is anxious to sell it. The man who has a nice home, has fixed it up and wants to live there would not sell that particular farm at $50 an acre; probably some would not sell at $100 an acre. But we are not placing on this farm the valuation that an individual would do who wanted to remain on a farm. Everyone in the vicinity knows that we desire to sell the farm. I venture to say, however, that we shall find it difficult to get as much money for the farm as we think it is worth.
Why sell it?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: But I would say that the offer which has been made is a fairly reasonable one and if we do not get a higher one we may some day sell it.

That seems to me to be quite a commentary on the position of agriculture in that section of the country as well as throughout Canada. I have from time to time from my place in the house advocated that the government should take some farm such as this and demonstrate to the farmers how

Supply-Agriculture
farming operations can be carried on at a profit in different parts of the dominion. It seems to me that might be done in this instance. The minister has stated that there are farms there where the owners are not anxious to sell that could not be bought for S50 an acre. On the other hand, he tells us that this farm probably would not sell for $20 an acre. This appears to me to be an excellent opportunity for the department to take the farm which they cannot get off their hands at a reasonable price and demonstrate to the farmers of that section just how they can farm profitably on a farm of that kind. After all, the farmers have to live on their holdings; whether those holdings are large or small, they have to meet their obligations and make enough to live on. It seems to me it would be a good idea if the government at this particular time would undertake to demonstrate to agriculturists just how they can, under present circumstances and with present prices of farm products, make a reasonable profit - out of a farm of that kind.
That, however, is not what I rose to discuss. A few moments ago the hon. member for Peel mentioned the fact that the agricultural college at Guelph had been handed over to the air force. I understand that from time to time there has been collaboration between the federal Department of Agriculture and the provincial departments along certain lines of experimentation. The minister might at this time give the committee some inkling of what is being done along that line; in what way the federal department is collaborating with the provincial departments, how much money is being expended in that way, and just what results are being obtained.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Certain activities are
being carried on in cooperation with the different provinces; they are not all the same in the different provinces. For example, we are carrying on soil surveys in certain areas in cooperation with the provinces, and we pay fifty per cent of the cost. Then we have investigations in connection with potatoes, for instance, diseases and methods of handling them. That is carried on in cooperation with the provinces. One could take almost any of the activities having to do with agriculture across Canada, and he would find that there is some cooperation between this department and the provincial departments of agriculture. For example, in the fighting of grasshoppers, we do the research and the province does the actual work of conducting the battle. The same thing is true with regard to fighting other pests; we do
the research work and the provinces do the actual work of putting the results of our research into practice. That runs all the way through the activities in connection with agriculture in the different sections.

Up to a certain point the
minister has been definite enough with his information, but I think it would be of interest and enlightening to the committee to know in just what directions there is cooperation between the federal and provincial departments of agriculture, not only by way of experiment but in other directions. There is a considerable vote here for experimental work of one kind and another, and it would be of interest to know what proportion of these votes is being used to collaborate with the provincial departments. The minister might enlarge considerably on his statement with regard to what is being done in that direction.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
I am afraid I would
be covering practically every vote there is in these estimates if I attempted to review all that is being done by the department in cooperation with the provinces. For example, our whole marketing service is carried on in cooperation with the provinces; we do the grading for the provinces. That is true of every section. If it is just in connection with experimental farm work that the question is asked, then I would say that the experimental work in connection with agriculture is carried on in cooperation with the provinces largely through such farms as the Guelph farm in Ontario where the agricultural college is situated, and through the colleges associated with the universities and some not in association with the universities. We subscribe certain funds toward the activities of the different professors in the colleges who are doing certain experimental work in connection with agriculture, such as soils, grasshoppers, fruit-growing; everything we are carrying on in Canada as related to agriculture. There is cooperation between the federal and provincial departments in experimental work, such as that associated with the handling of fruit. That is carried on only in provinces where fruit is grown, provinces like British Columbia, Ontario, and, to a certain extent, Quebec and the maritimes. The experimental work in connection with wheat and wheat tests is carried on largely in the prairie provinces, and we have in other provinces across Canada other activities in which there is cooperative effort.

Still the minister has not given me anything to indicate just what amount of this experimental farm vote is being spent
Supply-Agriculture

in that particular direction. May I say that I believe the experimental farms, not only those of the federal department, but also of the provinces, are doing very good work. If the minister cares to answer as to how much of this money is being expended in that way, he might at the same time indicate to the committee if any additional expenditures will be incurred by reason of the fact that the Guelph agricultural college, which he mentioned a short time ago, has been handed over for other purposes. Will that fact increase in any way the expenditures of the federal department in cariying on these experiments, or otherwise?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
The only activity which has been transferred from Guelph to any other point, for which we are expending a sum of money, has been transferred from Guelph to Vineland. That is only a very small amount.
In so far as the task the hon. member would like me to undertake is concerned, namely, that of segregating funds which are expended in cooperation with provinces or others, I am afraid that would be impossible. The staffs are working on the same type of work at the different places. Our staffs are engaged in doing work which is helpful to the provinces, and the provincial staffs are engaged in doing work which is helpful to us. There is, however, in the account, no segregation of the funds which would make it possible to answer the question in dollars.
I suppose it varies from year to year?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Yes.

The minister's statement with regard to the Rosthem farm and the value of the farm land surrounding it has been most interesting. I would judge that it is similar to the Indian Head farm, which he knows very well. The land around there is worth $75 or possibly $100 an acre. I believe farmers have refused that for it in days gone by. I understand the land on the Rosthem farm is extremely fertile, and is good country for farming. As the minister said, it is worth something over $50 an acre. The minister should assure the committee that this farm will not be sold at a price or value which could not be considered fair, even taking normal times into consideration. I think it should be worth at least $40 an acre. The minister should assure the committee that the government will not sacrifice the farm for $16 an acre, or anything like that. He mentioned a few minutes ago that it might be leased within the next week, or that it might be taken over, or some deal made with the provincial government. He should give us information with

regard to that. How far have negotiations with the provincial government proceeded? I believe a good deal more information is due to the committee.

May I say a word with regard to the value of land to-day. I do not think there is any more difficult job in western Canada than that of estimating present-day land prices. Some people tell us that land has very little or no value; others tell us that it has a high value. For example, the loan companies send in their agents or valuators. I have had them come to my district. One man would value a piece of land at $40 an acre. Then probably the next day, along would come another valuator, from another company, and he would value it at SS or $10 an acre.
' When you ask a man, under present conditions, to come in and say what the value of a piece of land should be, and when he has to take into account future prospects with regard to wheat prices, and the fact that there have been crop failures in western Canada, he has before him an extremely hard job. Land companies in western Canada have a tendency to hold up prices, or to try to keep them up where they were some years ago. Other companies, or other people are endeavouring to keep prices down to figures they believe to be right and fair. That is happening under the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act.
Not long ago I heard men say in western Canada that there is no land there worth more than $10 an acre, because, in their opinion, the land is worth only the return it will bring. They urge that under present prices, and having in mind present prospects of future markets, a farm will earn not more than $10 an acre. Be that as it may, we hope and trust that, in the future, market prices for our farm products in western Canada will improve.
They will.

I can understand that in these circumstances the Department of Agriculture is not anxious to give away this land. I have land for which I have been offered a low price. People have been trying to get me to sell it; but I am hanging on to it, and trying to keep it, although it is not being farmed to the greatest extent, particularly since the cut in wheat acreage. We hope, however, that future conditions will be better. I presume that is the way the Department of Agriculture are looking at the matter, so far as it affects the farm at Rosthern. They are hoping for better conditions in the future, and that they will be able to get better prices.

Supply-Agriculture

Better prices will come
with a new government.

The minister has not commented on the suggestion made by the hon. member for Haldimand which, it seems to me, had a good deal of merit. In the minds of a great manjr farmers, officials in the Department of Agriculture are out of touch with the real problem of farming. It would be a worth-while gesture if some of the officials in the department would undertake to farm the experimental farm at Rosthern, and attempt to demonstrate that farming can be made profitable under present conditions. I should like to hear what the minister has to say, or as to whether he has considered calling on volunteers from his department to undertake an experiment of this sort.
How about summerfallowing?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
There is only one thing I should like to say, and it is this: I do not think any experiments carried on by the government to try to demonstrate how one can run the farm at Rosthern would be beneficial either to the government or to the people in the surrounding district. The farmer who operates a farm in a community, and who makes a success of it, is the best guide to any farmer in the neighbourhood as to what it costs, and how a farm can best be run. The government, with the whole credit of the country behind it, attempting to operate a farm, is not in any sense in the same position as the individual farmer who is running his farm privately. Anything which the government might do might not be done by the ordinary farmer in carrying on his activities on such a farm.
Experiments have, however, been carried on not very far from Rosthern by an official who was for a number of years closely associated with this department-if he is not even yet-working with the department of agriculture of Saskatchewan. He is a brother of Doctor Kirk, who is at present in charge of a department in the agricultural college at Saskatoon. He operated a farm at Lockwood, which is not far removed from Rosthern. That farm was operated for the Saskatchewan government. It was a poor piece of land; that is, it was light, and sandy. I believe he gave as good a demonstration as could be given by a person hired by a government as to what it costs to operate on such land, and what can be done with land which is really under the average in value. I doubt very much if it had any
real value to the people living in that or other sections. He did as good a job as could be done.
We, on the other hand, attempt to give some demonstrations to farmers by having areas of certain farms rented, and by giving instructions to farmers in the community as to how to run those particular sections of their farm. Some demonstrations are given on those plots, and they are beneficial to persons operating their own farms in the immediate vicinity. But as to taking over Rosthern farm, with its decorative shrubs and all that kind of thing, and putting a farmer on it and telling him to operate it to prove to the farmers around what it costs to run a farm-well, I am afraid it would not be very successful.

When this item was first
brought up I was attending a committee in another part of the building. Therefore I am not sure just what has been said up to now. I believe the question has been raised as to why this farm has not been sold.
Why it should not be.

I do not know whether
hon. members on this side of the house, who sit in opposition, have supported the selling of the farm. Last year I was against the sale of this farm, and I am just as much against it this year. I am quite satisfied that the hopes of the department so far as the saving of money is concerned have not been and will not be realized to any great extent. Most of the people drawing any salary to speak of at all have had to be moved to other farms and still remain on the payroll. So far as I can see, about the only money that will be saved is in connection with the few people who vTere working by the hour at no large wage and who were recruited from the town of Rosthern. As I pointed out at that time, there would not be a large saving through closing the farm.
If the dominion government feel, as apparently it does, that the work which could be done on this farm is something which should be carried on, not by the federal government but by the provincial government, I suggested and still hope they can get the provincial department of agriculture to carry. on the important work this farm can do. I am sure that this farm can continue to do a great service by supplying foundation cattle stock to the district as well as foundation stock for the swine industry which is becoming more and more important all the time. I understand that the reason why the offer to buy this farm has r ot been accepted is that it is still hoped
Supply-Agriculture

that the provincial government will take over the farm and operate it as a foundation stock breeding and distributing station.
I am sorry that the government have seen fit to cease operating this farm as a federal experimental station, but I am glad that they have not disposed of it to a private individual. I understand they are still trying to get the provincial department of agriculture to operate it in the way I have mentioned. I hope that they will not dispose of the farm until every possible means has been explored to have the farm operated in the manner I have indicated. When the farm was closed they had a wonderful herd of Holstein cattle and people came from as far as two or three hundred miles away to get pure bred Yorkshire swine as foundation breeding stock for their farms. I am sure that if the provincial government took over this farm it would prove of great benefit to northern Saskatchewan, and the cost of operating it would be small compared with the amount of good that would accrue to the farming industry. I approve the government's attitude in not selling the farm.

The hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) has raised an interesting question, namely, whether this farm has been a paying proposition in years past and, if not, how much has been lost from year to year. I imagine that if it had been on a paying basis it would have been kept on by the department. This brings up the further question of operating these farms, as was suggested by an hon. member to my left and by myself. This farm could be operated as a demonstration farm to show how a farm of this kind could be operated at a profit. The minister says that it is impossible to do that, and I believe he is right. I have heard the statement made in years gone by, and it is still being made, that if farmers were to keep books, if they were to charge a reasonable price for their labour, property depreciation and everything else, as other businesses do, no one would ever put a plough in the ground. The minister might tell us whether this farm at Rosthern has been operating on a profitable basis and, if not, how much money has been expended from year to year over and above receipts.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
The cost of operating this farm over a term of jmars has varied from $14,000 to approximately $30,000. If I remember the figures correctly, last year we provided some $8,000, but it was thought that the farm would be operated for only part of the year. I think most hon. members realize that to make an expenditure of from $14,000 to $30,000 on a farm answers the question as to whether that farm can be 
operated, in the way in which the government operates it as an experimental farm, at a profit. I do not think there is any question that it could not be operated at a profit if experimental work is going to be carried on. The other question, as to whether the government could operate a farm and make it pay, is one which might arouse some curiosity. As I said a moment ago; however, I do not think it would prove anything.
Everybody knows the answer.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Some hon. member says, "everybody knows the' answer". Probably we would all give the same answer. That is a situation which I think can be dealt with only by experienced people who are carrying on farming in the way that an individual is compelled to carry it on. I doubt if the government going on to a farm and taking it over for the purpose of demonstrating whether it could be run at a profit or otherwise would be beneficial.
No one would expect an experimental farm to pay a direct profit.

I am not sure that it would not be beneficial. If the government undertook to operate a farm along the same lines as the average farmer and kept a system of books, it would show where the leaks and losses were to be found. I think everyone agrees that you cannot operate an experimental farm along the same lines as you would operate another farm so far as the question of profit and loss is concerned. I should, however, like to know whether the department has any idea of the loss incurred because of the experimental work done from year to year on this farm. We all realize that experimental work must entail a loss, but I should like to know to what extent that loss affects the revenues of the farm, what percentage of the loss incurred on that experimental farm or on the whole system of experimental farms would be due to the experimental work carried on.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture

speechtext: Has the minister given any consideration to the zoning of the agricultural resources of this dominion in respect of what might be profitably produced in one section of the country and unprofitably in another?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Zoning has been carried on by the farmers themselves in accordance with the natural conditions that exist in Canada, in addition to what the experimental stations demonstrate to be the proper thing to do. For example, they grow apples in the Annapolis valley.
We know that.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Yes, some people do, and apples are also grown in certain sections of Ontario and Quebec.
And British Columbia.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: To that extent the growing of apples is zoned.
That is twenty years old.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
In addition, we have zoning in connection with our cereal crops. We grow certain varieties, and within recent months we have been carrying on zoning in relation to the marketing of farm products. It was suggested a few months ago that we should establish one price for cheese all the way across Canada. We did not consider that that w7as good policy. We thought that cheese could be produced to advantage in certain areas of Canada and that in other areas it could not be produced to advantage. A certain flat price was established, and those producers who found it profitable to produce cheese have had their price increased by the giving of premiums or subsidies. The farmers in those areas can obtain a considerably better price for their cheese than farmers who undertook to produce cheese in areas that were
not so suitable. To that extent there has been recently, in relation to that particular product, some zoning which was not carried on previously. The same thing is more or less true in connection with the production of live stock across Canada.

That is a reasonably complete
answer by the Minister of Agriculture. It pretty well shows that there has been nothing done by the department so far as the zoning of agriculture in this dominion is concerned, and what has been done has been done by the producers themselves. As the minister has intimated it has been shown what can be produced economically in one section of the country and what can be produced economically in another section, but it is left to the producers themselves to work out their problems in their own individual way, so that they may produce economically what they have been producing at a loss.
It seems to me that we have been behind the eight-ball in agriculture in this dominion for a very long time. We have listened to discussions of ways and means of finding profitable production for certain products in certain sections. We have heard discussions of how it can be made profitable not to produce at all. In fact, we have had the spectacle of seeing our farmers paid not to produce.
I cannot help thinking that the Minister of Agriculture should give careful consideration to the zoning of agriculture in this dominion. He has been over a large portion of Canada. I do not know any farmer in Canada who has farmed the farmers more than has the present Minister of Agriculture. He has shown them all the ways and means by which they can vote for his party.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: More successfully than you did in Ontario.
Yes, but wait until your next test of public confidence comes, and it will be a greater debacle for you than I had in Ontario.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I have heard those prophecies before.

Wait until the next time comes. You have not had as much experience as I have.
Mr. GARDINER. I have been elected nine times.
True, but I do not know any farmer who is looked upon with more suspicion than the present Minister of Agriculture.

Shame.
Supply-Agriculture

It is no more shame to be looked upon in that way than for me to be referred to in that way. The present Minister of Agriculture is not infallible. We have had his maximum price for butter and to-day we have his minimum price for butter. He has changed right-about face. They say it is a smart politician who can turn twice in the one year, but the minister has changed his mind two or three times, so no wonder he is as smart as he thinks he is in gaining votes in Canada.
I say in all seriousness, Mr. Chairman, there has never been scientific zoning of agriculture in this dominion.
Why did you not do it between 1930 and 1935?

The Conservative party did more between 1930 and 1935 than the Liberal party has done since confederation, and that was when the Conservative party consummated the empire trade agreements in 1932 and stabilized the price of bacon and other products which we exported to the old land. Some hon. members shake their heads, but that type of member has been shaking his head ever since confederation. I am not playing that old dug-out kind of politics which the Liberal party and the Minister of Agriculture have played across this dominion. I say in all seriousness that the time has arrived when we should have a zoning policy for agriculture right across this dominion which would determine the zones in which certain products could be produced at a profit. Instead of that, the government's policy is to pay farmers $4 an acre not to produce at all.
What is the Conservative policy?

My hon. friend is not a farmer, but I have learned from experience that it is the man who knows the least about a particular subject who talks the most about it. My hon. friend looks more like a lawyer and acts more like a doctor of philosophy. Does my hon. friend know that to-day farmers are battling with their backs to the wall? If he did, he would not talk so lightly about farm problems. I know farmers in this country, whose sons are fighting overseas, who are battling with the various elements of nature, *who are battling with the weather itself to meet the obligations they have on their farm; farmers in northern Ontario, farmers in old southern Ontario, farmers who know that their mortgages are increasing steadily, farmers who are on stony land, on rough pasture land. If my hon. friend knows as much as he fMr. Howe.]
endeavours to imply that he knows about agriculture, he will know that the best pasture lands we have are the stony, rolling, rough lands, with brooks running through them, which cannot produce wheat. He will know as well those flat areas in Ontario which are not adapted to producing old fall wheat but are well adapted to the production of live stock on an economic basis. My hon. friend from Manitoba knows well that in his district he cannot produce wheat, but can produce live stock.
We produce both.

They produce both, he says. So can I, in the district which I represent. But I believe the time has long since passed when the farmers of this country should be left to zone their own districts. This is no new story as far as I am concerned. I have urged it upon successive predecessors of the present minister. I urged it upon the hon. gentleman from Melville; from 1930 to 1935 I urged upon the minister of the party to which I belong that we should zone this dominion; that we should set out in our bulletins from the Department of Agriculture those districts which are most adapted respectively to dairy production; to mutton, lamb and wool; to grain production, and to the production of fruit and other vegetable products; that, then, the Minister of Agriculture should coordinate his efforts with those of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, and no longer cling to this old and dusty free-trade doctrine by admitting fruit and vegetables into districts in which they compete with the local products.
We bonus western Canada for not producing wheat. Why should we build up in this dominion a lopsided agriculture, disregarding practically everything except wheat? I make that statement in all good faith. I have never pitted the west against the east. I produce, probably, as much wheat as the average Ontario farmer. Each year I grow between 75 and 100 acres of fall wheat, chiefly for the chaff and straw which it produces, and I feed the wheat, and have fed it for twenty years. I am not concerned about its price. I think I can get more benefit from feeding it to shorthorn cattle and Yorkshire hogs than by selling it in competition with the temporary price which is supported by the taxpayers of Canada.
In this country there are many districts now trying to grow wheat which would be better off if they produced live stock or dairy products. There are many other districts which would be better off producing mutton, lamb and v'ool products than in endeavouring

Supply

Agriculture
to raise dairy and beef products. There are a few districts in Ontario which can economically produce wheat. We are paying western Canada $4 an acre not to produce wheat because we have developed a lopsided farming industry, and on the other hand we are having absolutely no regard to the prospects of many other fertile districts. The minister should give some consideration to the zoning of districts in a systematic way. Bonusing is a vicious policy. I was one of the first to propose it in this chamber in a time of desperate economic conditions, back in 1932. The men who then condemned it are now the proponents of it.
I thought the hon. member said a minute ago that times were good back in 1932?

I never said they were good. The hon. member said they were bad. He did not need to tell the country that. Everybody knew it long before he did. In fact, if he had been in the business he would have recognized it as more serious than is indicated by his glib reference to it to-day. Nobody doubts that in 1932 times were bad. May I tell him that in 1929, and before his party left power in 1930, every grain elevator in Canada was bursting with unsold wheat, and every lumber yard was overflowing with unsold lumber. That depression did not come after 1930. In suggesting that it did, the hon. member is about fifteen years behind the times. In 1930 this country was facing a depression which started in ,1929. Any hon. member who is worthy of his place in this chamber knows that. The Minister of Agriculture laughs. Any man who knows the situation is well aware that the depression did not start in 1930; it began in 1929.
He knows it, too.
It did not end in 1930, though.

The Conservative party took office in 1930, as it did in every period since confederation when this country has faced a crisis, and let me tell hon. members opposite that we shall come into power again, because Canada is now heading for a depression. It was in 1929 that the stock-market debacle occurred. I heard hon. members on the front benches opposite say in 1929 that they were facing a crisis. The hon. member for York North laughs, but he knows what I say is true.

What about Dunning's May
day budget?

Yes, and Dunning's countervailing tariffs. The old free-trade party who said. "We will never raise tariffs," when the depression came along said, "We will set up a
countervailing tariff, and if tariffs are raised in Washington we will raise them too. We will do anything to avoid the depression which we see coming."
You and Dunning made a mess of it.

Don't say that of Mr. Dunning. You can say it of me. Mr. Dunning
is a better man than any you have at present.
I meant Mr. Bennett.

I thank the hon. member for associating me with Mr. Bennett, because either of us is better than the hon. member is. But, Mr. Chairman, do not let us make this discussion trivial. Let us take off this veil of camouflage. All intelligent men know that 1930 and 1932 were difficult years. There is not an hon. member to my left or to my right who is not aware of that. Every country in the world was going through difficulties at that time. In 1932 there were millions of men in the world -looking for jobs. During that period almost every country in the world changed its form of government.
We made a mistake.

Canada made a mistake, I will admit, in 1935 in changing from one government to the other. Mr. Chairman, could anyone, even my sceptical hon. friend, blame the situation of Canada in 1931 upon a party which had been only six months in power?
They promised to end the depression at once.

Yes, they promised to end the depression at once, but let me say this, in all frankness, that this party could never get into power if they did not start promising, because they saw their opponents living on promises. The Liberal party got into power and remained in power many years on promises. They promised to reform the senate.
Order. I must remind the hon. member that speeches in committee must be strictly relevant to the matter under consideration.

Mr. Chairman, I beg your
pardon. I realize we have gone far afield.
There are some farmers in the senate.

The questions which have been asked by hon. members to your right, sir, have diverted me from the issue which is before the committee. I submit in all fairness that if hon. members are not prohibited from asking questions that are irrelevant to
Supply-Agriculture

the issues before the committee, I should not be censured for answering such questions in a way that is relevant to present-day issues. I beg your pardon, Mr. Chairman, for having digressed so far, but I am trying to justify the position of the party to which I belong. I have urged upon the Minister of Agriculture on different occasions the desirability of zoning the great resources of this wonderful agricultural country, and I say to him in all seriousness that a careful survey should be made of the dominion to ascertain its potential resources. I am referring at the moment to fruit and vegetable production in Canada. I have been in sections of the great province of Quebec which are most adaptable to the raising of fruits and vegetable products. The minister has told me that they grow apples in Annapolis valley. Well, I have heard that before. He has told us that they grow apples in the valleys of Vancouver, and dandies at Indian Head.
And in Manitoba.

My hon. friend says they grow apples in Manitoba. We believe we grow some pretty good apples in Ontario. In fact, we have beaten all the rest of Canada with the apples that we have grown in northern Ontario. The hon. member for Peel will tell you, Mr. Chairman, that they grow excellent apples in his district. Coming from Simcoe county, although I do not wish to boast, I can say that we produce champion apples there. These areas might well be zoned with a view to finding out their capabilities; and, after the facts have been tabulated, I suggest that the minister should cooperate with the Minister of Trade and Commerce with a view to getting something done in this regard. One is sometimes skeptical about how closely these two ministers cooperate on questions that are of common interest to their respective departments.
We have a great opportunity in Canada to produce our own commodities, and it would give us justification for imposing a reasonable tariff upon seasonable products, such as fruit and vegetables, that are brought into the dominion. The minister might study conditions in the districts that can produce beef cattle economically. If he found this out, then he might devise ways and means of stopping the importation from the Argentine of anywhere from 18,000 to 20.000 head of cattle which enter Canada in tin cans.
Fifty thousand.

I thank the hon. gentleman for the interruption because the last time I looked it up the importation was not as great as that. Evidently, since his party came into

power, more beef cattle have been coming into the country in cans. The minister might well survey these possibilities.
I would go further and make this suggestion. We have a great deal of unsold wheat in our granaries. Every hon. member who has had anything to do with the production of live stock or live stock products knows that one can produce fats from live stock by the use of this unsold grain. I contend that a large portion of the wheat in the country should be diverted to the production of animal fats instead of bringing in fifty or sixty train loads of vegetable oils. Let there be no misunderstanding about this. I say, rip off the camouflage of political hypocrisy that surrounds the importation of millions of pounds of vegetable oils. We have radio broadcasts urging the women of the country, with a view to baking better cakes and buns, and getting rid of odours in the kitchen, to use Crisco and vegetable oils, while the farmers of Canada can produce animal fats, which are better in a cold climate like this. According to the best medical advice, they are better than vegetable oil.
Oh, no.

The hon. gentleman who
interrupts is not a doctor, but I see a doctor and he nods his approval. I repeat, we might as well be frank in these matters. If we are to develop Canada as a great agricultural country, we must realize-and I address this remark particularly to the free traders, who say that they will buy where they can get things the cheapest-that we are capable of producing our own commodities for our own people, and it would be far better for us to do so than to bring in 50,000 head of cattle in tin cans and fifty train loads of vegetable oils, only to supplant the animal fats that can be produced in Canada with the use of the grain that is unsold here.
Let me make this suggestion to the Minister of Agriculture. I would ask him to urge upon the cabinet taking 100.000,000 bushels of wheat out of the quantity lying unsold in our granaries and giving it to China. With her back to the wall, China is fighting a fourth enemy. As her premier said this morning, the Chinese can defend their country; they can defend their civilization against Japan if they are supported by necessary supplies of natural resources. As it is, the women and children of China are starving for wheat. They are eating rice.

I must remind the hon. gentleman that the item under discussion relates to the administration of experimental farms.

Supply-Agriculture

The item refers to experimental farms, but before the minister sat down he said that what he was most concerned about was to make the farms of Canada pay. I am trying to tell the committee how we can make our farms pay. If we can sell economically the wheat that is produced in western Canada as well as in other parts of the dominion, we shall make our farms pay.
I say to the minister, who I am sure is interested in this problem and who is responsible for the department that has to do with the great industry of agriculture in Canada, that he should urge upon his colleagues the presentation to China of 100,000,000 bushels of wheat free of charge and have it sent from the Pacific coast. That would do two things. First, it would support China in her desperate battle against a more highly organized power, and, second, it would cultivate in the Chinese a taste for wheat instead of rice. It would thus develop possible future markets for wheat, something that we have been trying for years to do.
